The first thing I remember is not a face or a room but the sound of rain on a tin roof. I was small enough to believe the sky had pockets. My grandmother said rain was the world remembering itself, each drop a syllable of some old story that had been told so many times it no longer needed a teller. I sat on the porch and watched the gutter become a river, carrying leaves and cigarette ash and a single yellow petal toward a drain that sounded, when the water rushed into it, like a patient swallowing. I thought if I listened closely I might hear the beginning of everything. I did not. I heard only rain, and beneath it, the refrigerator humming, and beneath that, my own heartbeat, which was already practicing the rhythm of departure.

Years later, I found a library that existed only in the hour before sleep. It had no card catalog, no librarian with spectacles and a stamp, only shelves that rearranged themselves according to what I was afraid of losing. On the shelf marked “Things I Meant to Say” were hundreds of blank index cards. On the shelf marked “People Who Left” were photographs taken from behind, everyone walking away, no faces, only shoulders and the backs of knees. I tried to check out a book called The Correct Thing to Do, but the pages were stuck together with honey. I woke with the taste of clover in my mouth and the certainty that I had forgotten something important, though I could not remember what.

There is a kind of loneliness that is not sad. It is a room with good light. You sit in it and the dust motes become tiny planets. You are not waiting for anyone. You are not missing anyone. You are simply aware that you are a temporary arrangement of atoms and that this is not a tragedy, only a fact, like the moon being far away. I have spent whole afternoons in that room. I have watched the shadow of a window cross the floor like a slow hand. I have thought about how much of life is just noticing. Then the phone rings, or the kettle whistles, and the room disappears, and you are back in the world of appointments and apologies and the terrible need to be understood.

I once tried to write a novel about a man who collected other people’s grocery lists. He would find them in shopping carts, on the ground outside supermarkets, tucked into library books. He kept them in a shoebox under his bed. He believed that a grocery list was the most honest autobiography a person could write. Milk, eggs, bread, tomatoes, aspirin, cat food, cheap wine. There was no room for lies. You could not pretend to be sophisticated when you needed toilet paper. The man never wrote his own list. He was afraid of what it would reveal. Eventually he fell in love with a woman who wrote hers in purple ink and always added one item that did not exist: “starfruit,” “ghost,” “a better tomorrow.” He never found her. He only found the lists.

If I could go back to any moment, I would not choose a graduation or a wedding or a first kiss. I would choose an ordinary Tuesday when I was nine. My mother was making soup. My father was reading the paper. My sister was drawing a horse with too many legs. The television was on mute. Outside, a neighbor was mowing his lawn. Nothing was happening. That is why I would choose it. I did not know then that nothing happening is the rarest thing of all. I did not know that one day I would trade a thousand fireworks for the sound of my mother’s spoon against a pot.

I am not good at endings. I leave the last sip of tea in the cup. I keep books with dog-eared pages because I cannot bear to finish them. I have friends I have not called in years because calling would mean admitting time has passed, and time passing means we are different, and different means the friendship I remember no longer exists. But sometimes I do call. We talk for an hour. We laugh at the same old jokes. We promise to do it again soon. We do not. But for that hour, the past and present sit together like two old men on a bench, not speaking, just watching the pigeons. That is enough.

Once, in a museum, I stood in front of a painting of a bowl of fruit for twenty minutes. It was not a famous painting. The apples were slightly bruised. The grapes were dusty. The tablecloth had a stain. I thought: someone painted this. Someone sat here and decided that this bowl, this ordinary bowl, was worth an entire afternoon. They mixed green and red and shadow. They thought about the curve of a pear. They made a decision about the light. And now, a hundred years later, I am standing here, and we are both thinking about the same pear. That is a kind of time travel. That is a kind of resurrection. Art is just attention that refuses to die.

So here I am, writing whatever comes to me, which is never whatever. It is always a trail of breadcrumbs leading back to the same few rooms: rain on a tin roof, a library before sleep, a grocery list in purple ink, a Tuesday with soup. I do not know what any of it means. I suspect meaning is not a destination but a side effect of paying attention. We are here for a short time. The light is good. The dust motes are planets. The kettle is about to whistle. And somewhere, a neighbor is mowing his lawn, and the world is remembering itself, one syllable at a time. I am trying, in my small way, to pay attention. That is all.

The first thing I remember is not a face or a room but the sound of rain on a tin roof. I was small enough to believe the sky had pockets. My grandmother said rain was the world remembering itself, each drop a syllable of some old story that had been told so many times it no longer needed a teller. I sat on the porch and watched the gutter become a river, carrying leaves and cigarette ash and a single yellow petal toward a drain that sounded, when the water rushed into it, like a patient swallowing. I thought if I listened closely I might hear the beginning of everything. I did not. I heard only rain, and beneath it, the refrigerator humming, and beneath that, my own heartbeat, which was already practicing the rhythm of departure. (127 maybe)

Paragraph 2:
Years later, I found a library that existed only in the hour before sleep. It had no card catalog, no librarian with spectacles and a stamp, only shelves that rearranged themselves according to what I was afraid of losing. On the shelf marked “Things I Meant to Say” were hundreds of blank index cards. On the shelf marked “People Who Left” were photographs taken from behind, everyone walking away, no faces, only shoulders and the backs of knees. I tried to check out a book called The Correct Thing to Do, but the pages were stuck together with honey. I woke with the taste of clover in my mouth and the certainty that I had forgotten something important, though I could not remember what. (124)

Paragraph 3:
There is a kind of loneliness that is not sad. It is a room with good light. You sit in it and the dust motes become tiny planets. You are not waiting for anyone. You are not missing anyone. You are simply aware that you are a temporary arrangement of atoms and that this is not a tragedy, only a fact, like the moon being far away. I have spent whole afternoons in that room. I have watched the shadow of a window cross the floor like a slow hand. I have thought about how much of life is just noticing. Then the phone rings, or the kettle whistles, and the room disappears, and you are back in the world of appointments and apologies and the terrible need to be understood. (127)

Paragraph 4:
I once tried to write a novel about a man who collected other people’s grocery lists. He would find them in shopping carts, on the ground outside supermarkets, tucked into library books. He kept them in a shoebox under his bed. He believed that a grocery list was the most honest autobiography a person could write. Milk, eggs, bread, tomatoes, aspirin, cat food, cheap wine. There was no room for lies. You could not pretend to be sophisticated when you needed toilet paper. The man never wrote his own list. He was afraid of what it would reveal. Eventually he fell in love with a woman who wrote hers in purple ink and always added one item that did not exist: “starfruit,” “ghost,” “a better tomorrow.” He never found her. He only found the lists. (135)

Paragraph 5:
The world is full of instructions we ignore. On a packet of seeds: “Do not plant in frozen ground.” On a bottle of medicine: “May cause drowsiness.” On a heart: “Handle with care.” We read them and nod and then do the opposite. We plant anyway. We drive anyway. We love people who are leaving anyway. I think this is not stupidity but hope, which is just stupidity with better posture. Hope says the frozen ground might thaw. Hope says drowsiness is a small price for dreaming. Hope says the heart is not glass; it is muscle, and muscle tears and heals and tears again, and that is how it grows. (106)

Paragraph 6:
If I could go back to any moment, I would not choose a graduation or a wedding or a first kiss. I would choose an ordinary Tuesday when I was nine. My mother was making soup. My father was reading the paper. My sister was drawing a horse with too many legs. The television was on mute. Outside, a neighbor was mowing his lawn. Nothing was happening. That is why I would choose it. I did not know then that nothing happening is the rarest thing of all. I did not know that one day I would trade a thousand fireworks for the sound of my mother’s spoon against a pot. (111)

Paragraph 7:
I have a theory that every city is a person who has forgotten their name. The streets are veins. The subway is a nervous system. The lights are thoughts that keep turning on and off. At night, the city dreams of the ocean it was built beside or the mountain it was built on or the river it buried. It wakes with a headache of traffic. It does not know why it is here. It only knows it must keep moving, keep growing, keep tearing down and building up, because stopping would mean remembering. And remembering would mean grieving. So it builds another glass tower and calls it progress. (109)

Paragraph 8:
I am not good at endings. I leave the last sip of tea in the cup. I keep books with dog-eared pages because I cannot bear to finish them. I have friends I have not called in years because calling would mean admitting time has passed, and time passing means we are different, and different means the friendship I remember no longer exists. But sometimes I do call. We talk for an hour. We laugh at the same old jokes. We promise to do it again soon. We do not. But for that hour, the past and present sit together like two old men on a bench, not speaking, just watching the pigeons. That is enough. (114)

Paragraph 9:
Once, in a museum, I stood in front of a painting of a bowl of fruit for twenty minutes. It was not a famous painting. The apples were slightly bruised. The grapes were dusty. The tablecloth had a stain. I thought: someone painted this. Someone sat here and decided that this bowl, this ordinary bowl, was worth an entire afternoon. They mixed green and red and shadow. They thought about the curve of a pear. They made a decision about the light. And now, a hundred years later, I am standing here, and we are both thinking about the same pear. That is a kind of time travel. That is a kind of resurrection. Art is just attention that refuses to die. (111)

Paragraph 10:
So here I am, writing whatever comes to me, which is never whatever. It is always a trail of breadcrumbs leading back to the same few rooms: rain on a tin roof, a library before sleep, a grocery list in purple ink, a Tuesday with soup. I do not know what any of it means. I suspect meaning is not a destination but a side effect of paying attention. We are here for a short time. The light is good. The dust motes are planets. The kettle is about to whistle. And somewhere, a neighbor is mowing his lawn, and the world is remembering itself, one syllable at a time. (110)
